notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Joshua after the land had been divided among the tribes of Israel. God told him it was time to establish the cities of refuge, carrying out the orders given earlier through Moses. God faithfully reminds his people to care for justice and protect human life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars think the cities of refuge were not established during Joshua's time, but were set up much later during King Josiah's religious reforms.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some older Catholic scholarship suggested that the three western cities date to the reign of Josiah, while the three eastern cities were added after the exile in Babylon.

notes.meaning: Joshua was instructed to have the Israelites pick out the special cities of refuge. God had already commanded this through Moses in the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. Christian readers often see these safe towns as a picture of the shelter and salvation believers receive in Jesus Christ.

These cities were opened to anyone who caused someone's death by complete accident. Running there protected the person from the avenger of blood, who was the dead person's nearest relative seeking justice. God's law made a clear difference between an unintentional tragedy and deliberate murder.

When a person ran to one of these cities, he had to stop at the city gate and explain what happened. The town elders sat at the gate, which served as the public courtroom. If the elders saw that the death was an accident, they welcomed him in and gave him a place to live.

If the relative seeking revenge caught up with the runner, the city leaders were strictly forbidden to hand him over. God commanded them to protect the person because he had acted without hatred or planning. This rule taught Israel to examine a person's motives carefully rather than acting out of hot anger.

The runner had to remain inside the city until the community could formally hear his case, and until the current high priest died. When the high priest died, the person was fully cleared to return home to his own family and land. Many commentators view the high priest's death as a picture of how Jesus' death frees us from the guilt of sin.

differ.view: The death of the high priest pictures the death of Jesus Christ, which frees believers from the penalty of sin.
The high priest's death was not a picture of Christ, but a national event of mourning where personal grudges were set aside.

notes.meaning: The people set apart three cities west of the Jordan River: Kedesh in the north, Shechem in the center, and Hebron in the south. Distributing them evenly across the land ensured that anyone in danger could reach safety quickly. These were also cities belonging to the Levites, which placed the runner among teachers who could guide and comfort him.

On the east side of the Jordan River, three more cities were selected: Bezer on the southern plateau, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan. Moses had chosen these towns before he died, and now they were officially opened for use. Having three towns on each side of the river meant help was close by for everyone.

These six cities were designated for every Israelite as well as for any foreigner living in the community. God's law provided the very same legal protection and justice to outsiders as to native citizens. No one accused of an accidental death was to be killed before receiving a fair trial before the assembly.
